Potawatomi

Potawatomi people continue through distinct nations and communities. Begin with Pokagon’s own historical account, Forest County’s selected institutional chronology and Citizen Potawatomi Nation’s explanation of the 1861 treaty. These community perspectives describe different paths through homeland continuity, removal pressures and political change.

Historical portrait of Simon Pokagon
Photographer unidentified · Chicago History Museum · Public domain

Source & image record ↗ · Public domain — Chicago History Museum’s explicit portrait-specific caption

The museum identifies the portrait as Simon Pokagon, a historical Potawatomi writer and leader, and explicitly labels that portrait public domain. Reuse as a named-person illustration within this broad people route, not a universal Potawatomi portrait or a picture of a present government. Existing exact asset and rights record retained. A museum-identified portrait of the named historical Potawatomi writer, not a portrait of the current Pokagon government or every Band citizen. The caption identifies its publication context as The City Beyond the White City: Simon Pokagon and The Red Man’s Rebuke/the Red Man’s Greeting, but does not name photographer or photograph date. Explicit Public domain statement applies to this portrait only, not other article images. Exact available full-frame JPEG copied unchanged; CSS crops and overlays affect card/backdrop display only.

Start reading here

A wider Potawatomi reading route with specific community examples, not a single government, interchangeable Band histories or a complete account.

  1. Our Culture / Neshnabé bmadzëwen — History

    Start with Pokagon’s selected community-authored history.

  2. Timeline of Potawatomi History

    Compare the selected Forest County institutional chronology, ending in 2005.

  3. 160th anniversary of becoming the Citizen Potawatomi - Potawatomi.org

    Read Citizen Potawatomi Nation’s dated explanation of 1861 and its distinct political path.

These are selected starting points. The full annotated collection, source perspectives, inspection limits and remaining research questions follow below. A starting guide is not an exhaustive history or community endorsement.

02

A path for deeper reading

Focus the next stage of research on: Bodéwadmi naming, language, Great Lakes homelands, removal and individual governments. The sources below are selected reading paths; their authorship, dates and community scope should guide how they are used.

Read the sources [1] potawatomi.org [2] potawatomi.org [3] fcpotawatomi.com

03

Keep community histories distinct

The Pokagon account presents its homeland continuity through removal pressure. Forest County’s selected timeline entries add a Wisconsin institutional perspective. These are related Potawatomi histories with different places and periods.

Read the sources [5] Pokagon Band of Potawatomi [6] Forest County Potawatomi Community

04

Compare the 1861 treaty account

Citizen Potawatomi Nation’s 2021 article describes different Citizen and Prairie Band choices and attributes an explanation of allotment and citizenship pressures to Kelli Mosteller. The treaty text and actual implementation remain separate reading tasks.

Read the sources [4] Citizen Potawatomi Nation

05

A named Potawatomi writer

The historical portrait shows Simon Pokagon, identified by the holding museum as a Potawatomi leader and writer. It accompanies this broader reading route as one named person, without representing all communities.

Read the sources [7] Chicago History Museum

Indigenous-ledCitizen Potawatomi NationSource 4

160th anniversary of becoming the Citizen Potawatomi - Potawatomi.org ↗

Publication: 2021-11-15

The Nation’s 2021 account attributes interpretation to Cultural Heritage Center director Kelli Mosteller and discusses the 1861 treaty, differing Citizen and Prairie Band choices, allotment and citizenship pressures. These are particular historical paths, not all Potawatomi experience.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Actual full article body, web lines 39–81 read. The underlying treaty and its implementation records were not inspected. Dated population and economic totals are not repeated.

Review recorded: October 27, 2026

https://www.potawatomi.org/blog/2021/11/15/160th-anniversary-of-becoming-the-citizen-potawatomi/

Community-authored cultural and historical accountPokagon Band of PotawatomiSource 5

Our Culture / Neshnabé bmadzëwen — History ↗

Publication: Undated; footer year is not treated as publication date

Substantive public history from a particular Potawatomi government. Useful for differences within related peoples and continuity through removal pressures. Legal summaries, casualty estimates and court details are not independently established here. Other ritual and clan sections are outside the selected synthesis.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Actual History section, web lines 511–522, and introductory culture paragraphs 499–503. Linked videos, archives and other sections not claimed as reviewed works.

Review recorded: October 21, 2026

https://www.pokagonband-nsn.gov/our-culture/

Community-published historical timelineForest County Potawatomi CommunitySource 6

Timeline of Potawatomi History ↗

Publication: Undated; latest displayed timeline entry 2005

A substantial community chronology, counted as one work. Selected institutional entries add a Wisconsin perspective rather than a universal Anishinaabe history. Origin dates, treaty totals, population figures and imprecise legal labels are excluded. The timeline's endpoint is not evidence of present operations.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Actual full timeline body read, web lines 59–171; synthesis uses 1937 and 1994–2002 institutional entries. A later same-day refetch timed out after successful initial inspection.

Review recorded: October 21, 2026
